comparison: Both evaluations support the model design and features (C6, C23-C30, C34, C40, C92-C93). OpenEval focuses on methodological consistency and design choices, while peer reviewers emphasize the model as 'state-of-the-art' and 'valuable' with 'convincing' evidence. Both note the model's public availability (C40).

Both evaluations support findings about amplitude modulation (C78-C80). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of Figure 7 showing phase effects are primary, while peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as part of the 'convincing' overall demonstration without raising specific concerns.

Both evaluations support the necessity of frequency and latency diversity (C60-C61, C64-C66). OpenEval details evidence from Figure 5, while peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the model shows 'complexity is necessary in terms of spatial configuration, frequencies and latencies' with 'convincing' evidence.

Both evaluations support findings about high-dimensional, stochastic responses (C54-C59, C67). OpenEval systematically analyzes Figure 4 results, while peer reviewers acknowledge the model 'shows that complexity is necessary' and 'considers the complexity of neural data.'

Both evaluations support cross-frequency coupling findings (C73-C77). OpenEval details Figure 6B simulations showing in-phase coupling produces realistic patterns, while peer reviewers explicitly mention cross-frequency coupling as a key finding with 'convincing' evidence.

Both evaluations support findings about slow component effects (C69-C72, C71-C72). OpenEval analyzes Figure 6A demonstrating the mechanism, while peer reviewers accept these as part of the cross-frequency coupling findings they describe as 'convincing.'

Both evaluations support the main findings about signal features enabling stable decoding (C8-C9, C38-C39). OpenEval summarizes collective evidence from Figures 3-7, while peer reviewers explicitly state authors 'identify' these requirements with 'convincing' evidence including oscillatory components and cross-frequency relations.

Both evaluations support findings about phase mechanisms (C36, C50-C53). OpenEval details Figure 3 evidence, while peer reviewers acknowledge the oscillatory component findings as part of the model's ability to 'capture empirical observations' with 'convincing' evidence.

Both evaluations support the limitation that standard decoding cannot distinguish mechanisms (C108-C109). OpenEval notes this as an 'important caveat,' while peer reviewers acknowledge 'there is no unambiguous mapping between neurobiological mechanisms and different signal generators.'

Both evaluations support the motivation regarding trial-level variability and stability (C83-C87, C10-C11). OpenEval notes these are well-accepted in neuroscience literature, while peer reviewers acknowledge the paper 'considers the complexity of neural data' and accepts the stochastic nature of responses.

Both evaluations support the model's ability to produce qualitatively similar TGMs (C7, C35, C50, C137). OpenEval notes the primarily qualitative nature of validation, while peer reviewers describe the model's ability to 'capture empirical observations' as 'convincing.'

Both evaluations express uncertainty about future applications and biological interpretation (C94, C96-C98, C31, C33). OpenEval marks these as 'speculative' about future utility, while peer reviewers express 'significant concern' about neurobiological interpretation and request 'more profound explanation' of conclusions.

Both evaluations support the acknowledged model limitations and simplifications (C99-C100, C102-C103, C105-C107). OpenEval notes these are 'appropriately speculative' and acknowledge limitations, while peer reviewers accept the transparency about limitations without challenge.

Both evaluations address the qualitative approach and parameter selection (C136, C143). OpenEval supports the decision not to optimize parameters given inter-subject variability, while peer reviewers express uncertainty, noting 'the power of the model is illustrated for only one specific set of parameters' and questioning whether different parameters could yield similar results.

Both address limitations in distinguishing mechanisms (C110). OpenEval marks future applications as uncertain/speculative, while peer reviewers explicitly support this limitation, acknowledging the ambiguity in mapping mechanisms to signal generators.

OpenEval supports the established decoding methodology and TGM interpretation (C19-C22, C44-C46, C121-C122). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these methodological claims.

OpenEval supports observations from real MEG data in Figure 2 (C47-C49, C69, C73, C141-C143). While peer reviewers reference the empirical TGM, they do not provide a separate evaluation of these specific observational claims.
OpenEval supports characterization of prior work and identified limitations (C88-C91). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these claims about prior literature.
OpenEval supports the illustrative Figure 1 and its qualitative comparison to real data (C117-C120). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these figure description claims.
